claim: Protein in food supplies nitrogen and the amino acids the body needs to build and maintain tissue; European regulators set the adult reference intake at 0.83 g of protein per kg of body weight a day.
unit: g protein per kg body weight per day
quote: the PRI for adults of all ages was estimated to be 0.83 g protein/kg body weight per day
notes: Second quote: "Dietary proteins are the source of nitrogen and indispensable amino acids which the body requires for tissue growth and maintenance." The FAO/WHO/UNU 2007 report (WHO TRS 935) gives the same adult safe level but could not be fetched (403), so it is not cited.

claim: Proteins are chains of amino acids; nine of them are essential (indispensable), meaning the body cannot make them and must get them from food.
quote: An amino acid the body cannot make and must get from food.
notes: Quote is the package glossary definition GL-003. FAO 2013 Table 5 lists histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine plus cysteine, phenylalanine plus tyrosine, threonine, tryptophan and valine.

claim: Protein quality is scored by how well a food supplies digestible essential amino acids: PDCAAS is the older score, capped at 1.0 (100%); DIAAS is the newer score FAO recommended in 2013, which is not capped and uses digestibility of each amino acid.
quote: A new protein quality measure (digestible indispensable amino acid score; DIAAS) is recommended to replace PDCAAS.
notes: Second FAO quote: "Values above 100% should not be truncated as was done for the PDCAAS value." PDCAAS-like scores flatter plant proteins against DIAAS [NQR-15].

claim: Measured in growing pigs, soy protein isolate scores a DIAAS of about 97, pea protein concentrate 70 and brown rice protein 42, against 113 to 137 for pork products; human data can be lower than pig data.
unit: DIAAS, older child and adult pattern
quote: Soy isolate is the reference: measured pig DIAAS of 97 on the older child and adult pattern
notes: Quote from package app-j (J.2). Mung bean digestibility in Indian children was about 20% lower than pig estimates [SCI-42]. Values are per ingredient; blends score higher than their weakest part.

claim: Labels and feed specifications often give "crude protein", which is nitrogen multiplied by 6.25 and so also counts non-protein nitrogen such as the nucleic acids that are abundant in microbial biomass.
quote: Nitrogen content multiplied by 6.25; includes non-protein nitrogen such as nucleic acids.
notes: Package glossary GL-002. Matters when reading single-cell protein figures of 70 to 84% crude protein.

claim: In this study, alternative protein means protein for food or feed made from plants, microorganisms, fungi, algae, insects or cultivated cells rather than conventional livestock and fish.
quote: Protein for food or feed made from plants, microorganisms, fungi, algae, insects or cultivated cells rather than conventional livestock and fish.
notes: Package glossary GL-001. Note the definition explicitly includes feed.

claim: In the European Union a novel food is one not eaten to a significant degree in the EU before 15 May 1997; it needs pre-market authorisation.
quote: Food that had not been consumed to a significant degree by humans in the EU before 15 May 1997
notes: Quote re-read on the European Commission page on 2026-09-25. Legal basis Regulation (EU) 2015/2283. Traditional foods from third countries have a notification route (package app-g).

claim: In Singapore a novel food is food without a history of use as food over the past 20 years, including cultivated meat and precision-fermented proteins; selling an unapproved novel food has been an offence since 28 November 2025.
quote: Novel food comprises food or food ingredients that do not have a history of use as food over the past 20 years.
notes: Quote re-read on the SFA page on 2026-09-25 (same URL as EXP-34 and REG-63).

claim: In the United States many new ingredients reach market as GRAS (generally recognised as safe by qualified experts), which is not subject to FDA pre-market approval; notifying FDA is voluntary, and FDA proposed tighter oversight on 10 August 2026.
quote: not subject to premarket review and approval by FDA
notes: Fragment quoted from the FDA GRAS page (fetched 2026-09-25). An FDA "no questions" letter is not a formal approval. Cultivated meat follows a separate FDA consultation plus USDA inspection (package APR-019 notes).

claim: Vietnam has no novel-food category: no law or decree defines novel food, history of safe use or pre-market assessment for a new food source.
quote: Vietnam has no novel-food category. No law or decree defines novel food, history of safe use or a pre-market safety assessment
notes: Quote from package app-g. The July 2026 draft Food Safety Law summaries do not add one [REG2-05; REG2-06].

claim: Plant protein ingredients are graded by purity: concentrates hold about 60 to 80% protein and isolates about 90% or more; textured vegetable protein is made by extrusion (cooking and shaping under heat and pressure), and high-moisture extrusion makes fibrous whole-cut analogues.
source_ids: glossary GL-007; glossary GL-008; glossary GL-011; glossary GL-044; glossary GL-045
quote: A protein ingredient of about 60 to 80% protein.
notes: Package glossary GL-008 (concentrate); GL-007 (isolate): "A protein ingredient of about 90% protein or more."

claim: Traditional plant proteins are modest in protein per 100 g: tofu has 10.9 g in the Vietnamese food composition table, against 19.0 g for lean pork and 20.3 g for chicken; shop labels for tofu often show less.
quote: Label protein is below the FCT value of 10.9 g (DPP-016 disagreement in the package).
notes: Quote from package data (protein_food_micronutrients.csv). Retail-audit tofu labels had a median of 4.98 g per 100 g (n = 5); the package gives both and does not average.

claim: Tempeh, whole soybeans fermented with Rhizopus mould, holds about 17 to 25% protein.
quote: The protein content of tempeh ranges from 16.65-25.19%
notes: Small regional journal; six soybean varieties and three fermentation times; basis probably as eaten (moisture about 60 to 67%).

claim: On Vietnamese shelves, dried textured soy (TVP) is about 64 g protein per 100 g as sold, while gluten or TVP-based chay analogues hold 12 to 25 g per 100 g once hydrated; every locally made product with 10 g or more of protein uses imported textured soy, soy concentrate or wheat gluten.
quote: gluten- or TVP-based analogues at 12 to 25 g per 100 g hydrated (median 19 g)
notes: Quote from package ch04. 64 g is the median of 5 dried chunks (protein_food_micronutrients.csv NQR-MN18). Convenience sample, not a market survey.

claim: The best-known modern plant-based burgers both reached market in 2016: the Beyond Burger, sold in the meat case, and the Impossible Burger, first served on 27 July 2016 at Momofuku Nishi in New York.
quote: It will introduce the Impossible Burger on Wednesday, July 27, at Momofuku Nishi in Manhattan.
notes: Beyond quote: "The company introduced the Beyond Burger in 2016 ... sold in the meat case." Both are company statements. The 2016 Impossible recipe: water, wheat protein, coconut oil, potato protein and leghemoglobin.

claim: Modern plant-based meat is mature technology but its market has shrunk from the 2021 peak: in the US its share of meat dollar sales fell from 1.4% (2021) to 0.7% (2025), and Beyond Meat revenue from USD 465 million to USD 276 million; global retail sales were about USD 6.6 billion in 2025.
unit: % of US meat sales; USD billion
quote: USD 88 million (2018), USD 465 million (2021 peak), USD 276 million (2025)
notes: Beyond Meat quote from package working paper wave6/global. US and global sales data are licensed Circana, SPINS and Euromonitor figures published by GFI (advocacy). Global figure confidence Medium.

claim: Textured plant protein is cheap to make: our package estimates dry TVP at about USD 790 to 2,070 per tonne ex-factory in Vietnam, and Chinese textured protein arrives at about USD 1.6 to 1.7 per kg; no verified capital-cost benchmark for extrusion was found.
source_ids: COST-01; COST-21; COST-28; FORM-05; FORM-06; FORM-07
quote: puts dry TVP from soy flour or concentrate at USD 790 to 2,070 per tonne ex-factory
notes: Quote from package app-j (J.2); a package calculation, not a market price. Chinese export prices from package ch04 (2023 data, High).

claim: Traditional fermentation uses moulds and bacteria to transform food: koji mould (Aspergillus oryzae) makes soy sauce, miso and Vietnamese tuong; it cannot make aflatoxin, although wild starters still need safety checks.
source_ids: glossary GL-025; glossary GL-031; glossary GL-032; SCI-19
quote: A. oryzae cannot make aflatoxin, because its aflatoxin gene cluster carries disabling mutations.
notes: Quote from package app-j (J.4). A. oryzae can make cyclopiazonic acid and 3-nitropropionic acid, so strains need characterising [SCI-19].

claim: Mycoprotein, sold as Quorn, is a fungus (Fusarium venenatum) grown in fermenters fed with glucose, ammonia and salts; it went on sale in the UK in 1985 and is now sold in about 17 to 20 countries.
quote: the main component of Quorn foods which was launched in 1985 ( 4 ) and is now sold in twenty different countries
notes: Disagreement: UK approval year given as 1984 [PRA-03] or 1981 [PRA-04]; launch year 1985 agreed. Country count 17 [PRA-06, 2019] or 20 [PRA-03, 2023]. PRA-03 quote trimmed of a trademark symbol.

claim: Mycoprotein is about 12% protein as harvested (wet) and 30 to 45% on a dry basis, scores a PDCAAS of about 1.0, and needs a heat step that cuts its RNA from about 10% to 2% of dry weight.
quote: Freshly harvested mycoprotein has a protein content of 12% ( w / w , wet weight)
notes: Wet and dry figures describe the same product on different bases; they do not disagree. RNA quote from package app-j: "falls from about 10% to about 2% of dry weight after a 68 C, 20-minute heat step".

claim: A peer-reviewed cost model puts mycoprotein at USD 29.56 per kg of protein, able to match beef but not chicken; the largest biomass-protein capacity is in China (Angel Yeast 11,000 t a year; Cabio with Nourish about 170,000 t of finished product).
unit: USD per kg protein; t per year
quote: will not be an economic alternative for inexpensive products such as chicken
notes: Cost quote from package app-j (Risner et al. 2023, High). Chinese capacity figures from press and GFI APAC (advocacy), Medium. A plant costing USD 100 million in the US costs about USD 15 million in China [HSC-13].

claim: Single-cell protein for feed is not new: ICI ran a 1,500 m3 Pruteen reactor from 1979 to 1987, and its product sold at about twice the price of soy protein.
quote: ICI's 1,500 m3 Pruteen feed-SCP reactor ran from 1979 to 1987 and sold at about twice the price of soy protein
notes: Quote from package app-j (J.5). A useful precedent: technical success, commercial failure against soy.

claim: Gas fermentation grows bacteria on gases instead of sugar: Solar Foods makes Solein from hydrogen and CO2 (approved in Singapore in 2022) in a plant of at most 160 to 230 t a year, with a 3,200 t plant planned for late 2028 but not yet financed.
source_ids: COST-53; FTG-04; FTG-05; RGN-04; glossary GL-027
quote: Largest plant 160 to 230 t a year (Finland); first commercial plant (3,200 t a year) planned for late 2028
notes: Quote from package ch16. Company says 160, press 230; the package gives both. Singapore date 29 Sep 2022 (package approvals.csv APR-004). Modelled cost EUR 4.0 to 4.5 per kg protein in 2030 at best sites [FTG-01].

claim: Bacterial protein for feed is sold at scale in China: Clostridium protein from steel-mill off-gas (about 84% crude protein) was certified in 2021 and made 10,200 t in 2023, while Calysseo's 20,000 t a year methane-protein (FeedKind) plant halted in 2026.
unit: t in 2023; t per year capacity
quote: Shougang LanzaTech made 10,200 t of protein in 2023, at 0.1 to 0.15 t per t of ethanol
notes: Quote from package app-v. Unibio plans 50,000 t a year in Saudi Arabia from 2028 [FTG-07], a plan not a plant. Clostridium protein replaces about 30% of fishmeal in shrimp without growth loss [SCI-23].

claim: Precision fermentation, engineered microbes making one specific protein, is decades old in medicine and cheese: recombinant human insulin was approved in the US in 1982 and fermentation-made chymosin (rennet) was affirmed safe for food in 1990.
source_ids: PRA-10; PRA-07; PRA-08; PRA-09; glossary GL-023
quote: Humulin, a recombinant human insulin fabricated in the bacterium E. coli [ 35 ], was the first approved biopharmaceutical (by the FDA) in 1982
notes: Chymosin: eCFR source note "55 FR 10935, Mar. 23, 1990". The share of cheese or rennet now made with fermentation-produced chymosin is given as over 90% of rennet [PRA-09] or about 70% (US) and 90% (UK) of cheese [PRA-08]; years not stated; do not average.

claim: Precision-fermented proteins reached food mainly as small, high-value ingredients: FDA raised no questions on Impossible Foods' yeast-made heme protein in 2018 (up to 0.8% of a burger) and on Perfect Day's whey protein in 2020, and Singapore approved Remilk's whey protein in 2023.
quote: use at a level up to 0.8% soybean leghemoglobin protein to optimize flavor in ground beef analogue products
notes: Perfect Day letter quote: "We have no questions at this time regarding Perfect Day's conclusion that beta-lactoglobulin is GRAS". EFSA also issued an opinion on soy leghemoglobin in 2024 [SCI-09].

claim: Precision fermentation is not yet cheap enough for bulk protein: experts say yields above 50 g per litre are needed, the best published heme yield is 10.1 g per litre, and no peer-reviewed cost model for a food protein was found.
quote: The cost-efficiency requirements involve production titers above 50 g/L
notes: Quote from package app-j (Nielsen et al.). The 50 g/L figure is an expert assertion, not a modelled threshold. Scale reference: a 600 m3 US plant starting 2026 [COST-54]; funding share of precision fermentation within fermentation rose from 33% (2023) to 66% (2025) [FTB-17, advocacy].

claim: Cultivated meat is grown from animal cells: a small starter population is multiplied in growth medium (nutrients plus signalling proteins called growth factors) in bioreactors, and may be grown on edible scaffolds to form tissue.
unit: cells per batch for about 1 t of meat
quote: as cell number grows, the culture is gradually moved to bioreactors with controlled conditions such as temperature, pH and dissolved oxygen
notes: Post et al. 2020: seed train from "typically in the order of 10^4 cells" to "10^13 cells, to create 1 ton". Growth factors can be up to 95% of serum-free medium cost at current prices [SCI-15].

claim: The first cultivated beef burger was cooked and tasted in public in London on 5 August 2013.
quote: Cultured meat has evolved from an idea and concept into a reality with the August 2013 cultured hamburger tasting in London.
notes: Exact day (5 August) from PRA-22, which cites press sources.

claim: Singapore was the first country to approve cultivated meat (Eat Just chicken, 26 November 2020), with first sales in December 2020; by August 2026 Singapore listed six cultivated products and the US FDA had completed five consultations, including salmon in May 2025.
unit: year of first approval and sale
quote: Singapore lists six cultivated products, including the world's first cultivated duck (April 2026) and beef (July 2026)
notes: Quote from package app-j (J.11). Approval date from package approvals.csv APR-002. GOOD Meat reported more than 2,000 servings sold from December 2020 to May 2024 [NOV-10], a company claim (Low).

claim: Cultivated-meat cost estimates differ by an order of magnitude: Humbird's 2021 model gives USD 37 to 51 per kg of wet cells and judges food prices unlikely, while a GFI-commissioned CE Delft model gives USD 5.66 per kg by 2030 under optimistic assumptions.
quote: USD 37/kg of wet cell mass in fed-batch (24 x 20 m3 reactors, 6.8 kt/yr) and USD 51/kg in perfusion
notes: Quote from package app-j. CE Delft quote: "$5.66 per kg ($2.57 per pound)" (advocacy summary, report not read). They differ mainly on growth-factor prices, achievable cell density and reactor cost [SCI-14; SCI-15]. A 50:50 cell and plant hybrid was modelled at USD 13.67 per kg [SCI-16; SCI-17]. Give all; do not average.

claim: Cultivated meat remains tiny in 2026: the largest production run is 20,000 litres, specialised firms fell from 155 to 142, investment fell to about USD 74 million in 2025 from about USD 1 billion in 2021, and an expert panel gave a 54% chance world output stays below 100,000 t a year through 2051.
quote: Largest run 20,000 L; Believer Meats shut in December 2025 after FDA clearance; firms fell from 155 to 142
notes: Quote from package ch16. FTB-24 and CAP-51 are GFI (advocacy) data. Believer Meats shut after regulatory clearance, so approval is not the binding constraint [FTB-24].

claim: Microalgae such as spirulina and chlorella are 50 to 70% protein by dry weight and are sold mainly as supplements; no DIAAS for microalgal biomass had been published as of a 2021 review.
quote: Species such as Arthrospira platensis and Chlorella vulgaris contain protein levels ranging from 50% to 70% of their dry weight
notes: Singapore approved Chlamydomonas algae biomass in 2019 [RGN-04]. Vietnam has grown spirulina at Vinh Hao since about 1976 (company claim, Low) [ECO-52].

claim: Duckweed (tiny floating plants) holds roughly 20 to 44% protein depending on species and growing conditions; the EU judged a Lemna protein concentrate safe in 2023 but could not confirm the safety of whole Wolffia powder because of manganese.
quote: Wolffia protein is 20 to 30% of freeze-dried weight across 11 laboratory-grown species
notes: Quote from package app-j. Thai Wolffia held 44.3% crude protein [SCI-35, VN-adjacent, Medium]; give both.

claim: Insect meal, mainly black soldier fly larvae, is already sold as feed, including from a 10,000 t a year plant in Vietnam opened in 2023; in shrimp it replaced 20% of fishmeal without loss but 30% reduced growth. This study treats insects as a benchmark only.
unit: t per year; % of fishmeal replaced
quote: 10,000 t/yr in Ho Chi Minh City (former Ba Ria-Vung Tau), opened 23 November 2023
notes: Quote from package ch04. Entobel H-Meal is at least 53% crude protein. Output not disclosed. Package framing: insects are never recommended.

claim: Hybrid products mix animal and alternative protein: the only cultivated chicken sold in Asian retail (Singapore, 2024) contained 3% cultivated cells, and soy is already the standard extender in processed meat.
source_ids: NOV-10; NOV-11; glossary GL-019; glossary GL-203
quote: 3 percent cultivated cells
notes: Quote from package source note for NOV-10. In a blended minced-pork dish with 20 to 30% of protein from textured soy, DIAAS stays at or above about 97 (package app-j calculation). Consumer evidence mixed: about half would rather not buy 70/30 hybrids [HXE-09].

claim: Most of the world's soy is eaten by animals, not people: about 77% of global soy is fed to livestock, 87% of soybeans are crushed into oil and meal, 99% of that meal goes to feed, and only about 6% of soy is eaten directly as food.
quote: More than three-quarters (77%) of global soy is fed to livestock for meat and dairy production.
notes: Second quote (PRA-20): "87% of the global soy output is processed into soy oil and soy cake". Underlying data USDA PSD. 7% of soy is fed whole to animals (OWID footnote).

claim: Fishmeal, the high-quality protein in shrimp and fish feed, is limited to about 4 to 4.5 million tonnes a year, and aquaculture uses most of it.
unit: Mt per year; % used in aquaculture
quote: About 4.5 Mt of fishmeal was made in 2016, 69% of it used in aquafeed
notes: Quote from package app-h. A 2026 paper gives about 87% used by aquaculture, citing FAO 2024 [FM-35]. Different years; give both.

claim: Feed ingredients set the price to beat: in August 2026 a tonne of protein cost about USD 880 in soybean meal against USD 3,846 in fishmeal (USD 2,625 in 2025).
quote: soybean meal protein cost about USD 880 per tonne in August 2026 against USD 3,846 for fishmeal protein
notes: Quote from package app-j (J.5), derived from World Bank Pink Sheet prices and protein contents.

claim: In Vietnam, feed is the most advanced alternative-protein market (insect meal and imported Chinese microbial protein are already sold), and almost all soybeans are imported: 2.61 Mt in 2025, 98.4% of supply.
quote: Vietnam imported 2.61 Mt of soybeans in 2025, 98.4% of supply
notes: Quote from package app-j (J.2). Feed-market statement from package ch04: "The most advanced alternative-protein market in Vietnam is animal feed".
